posts.title: What Is a Robot? A Beginner’s Guide to Robotics
posts.summary: Learn what robots are and how they work. This article introduces sensors, motors, microcontrollers, and batteries, explains how robots sense, decide, and move, and uses familiar examples and simple Arduino code to help beginners get started.
posts.description: A beginner-friendly introduction to robots, their essential components, how they sense and move, real-world examples, and simple Arduino experiments.

blocks.text: A robot is a programmable machine that can sense its surroundings, process information, and perform physical actions. Some robots work independently, while others follow commands from a person. What makes a machine a robot is the connection between sensing, decision-making, and movement.
The basic parts of a robot

items: Sensors collect information about the environment. Cameras, ultrasonic sensors, touch switches, and temperature sensors are common examples.
A microcontroller or computer reads sensor data and decides what the robot should do. Arduino boards and Raspberry Pi computers are popular beginner platforms.
Actuators create movement. DC motors drive wheels, servo motors rotate to a precise angle, and robotic grippers open or close.
A power source, such as a battery pack, supplies energy to the controller, sensors, and motors.
The mechanical structure holds all components together and determines how the robot moves and interacts with objects.

blocks.text: How a robot works

Most robots repeat a simple cycle: sense, decide, and act. A sensor first measures something in the environment. The controller compares that measurement with programmed rules. It then sends a command to a motor, light, buzzer, or another output. The cycle repeats many times every second.

items: Sense: collect data from the environment.
Decide: process the data using programmed logic.
Act: control motors or another output.
Repeat: measure the result and respond again.

blocks.text: Robots you may already know

items: Robot vacuum cleaners map rooms, detect walls, and plan cleaning routes.
Delivery robots use cameras, GPS, and obstacle sensors to move packages safely.
Factory robots repeat precise movements for welding, assembly, and inspection.
Mars rovers use cameras, scientific instruments, wheels, and remote commands to explore another planet.

blocks.text: Your first Arduino output
An LED is a simple actuator because the Arduino can turn it on or off. Upload this sketch to blink the built-in LED on most Arduino boards.
Read a simple sensor
This sketch reads a push button on pin 2 and turns on the built-in LED while the button is pressed. It demonstrates the sense-decide-act cycle in its simplest form.
Where to go next

Once you understand inputs, decisions, and outputs, you can combine an ultrasonic sensor with motors to build an obstacle-avoiding robot. Start with one component at a time, test each connection, and expand the program only after the current step works reliably.

posts.title: How to Make a Simple LED Project with Arduino
posts.summary: Start your robotics journey by blinking an LED. Learn what an Arduino is, how to connect an LED and resistor, and how a short program brings hardware and software together.
posts.description: Step-by-step instructions for wiring and programming a beginner Arduino LED project.
posts.imageAlt: Arduino LED circuit on a breadboard

blocks.text: Blinking an LED is a small project, but it teaches the complete workflow used in larger embedded and robotics systems: build a circuit, configure a pin, upload a program, observe the result, and improve the behavior.
What you need

items: Arduino Uno or a compatible board
One LED
One 220 Ω or 330 Ω resistor
Breadboard and jumper wires
USB cable and the Arduino IDE

blocks.text: Connect the circuit

items: Disconnect USB power while building the circuit.
Connect Arduino digital pin 8 to one end of the resistor.
Connect the other end of the resistor to the LED’s longer leg, called the anode.
Connect the LED’s shorter leg, called the cathode, to an Arduino GND pin.
Check the LED direction and connections, then reconnect the USB cable.

blocks.text: The resistor limits current and protects both the LED and the Arduino output pin. Do not connect an external LED directly between pin 8 and ground without a resistor.
Upload your first program
How the code works

The setup function runs once and configures pin 8 as an output. The loop function runs repeatedly. HIGH applies voltage to the LED circuit, LOW removes it, and delay pauses the program for a number of milliseconds. A delay of 1000 means one second.
Try a faster blink
Change both delay values to 200 and upload the sketch again. The LED will blink five times faster.
Troubleshooting

items: If the LED does not light, rotate it because LEDs work in only one direction.
Confirm that the correct board and serial port are selected in the Arduino IDE.
Check that pin 8 in the circuit matches ledPin in the program.
Make sure the jumper connected to the short LED leg reaches GND.

blocks.text: You have now controlled a physical component with software. The same idea scales to buzzers, relays, motors, displays, and complete robots.

posts.title: Run Your First Obstacle-Avoiding Robot
posts.summary: Build a simple autonomous robot with an Arduino, ultrasonic sensor, motor driver, and DC motors. Learn how it measures distance, decides when to turn, and navigates around obstacles.
posts.description: A beginner-friendly obstacle-avoiding robot project with components, circuit connections, control logic, and Arduino code.

blocks.text: An obstacle-avoiding robot is an excellent first autonomous system. An ultrasonic sensor measures the distance ahead, the Arduino decides whether the path is clear, and a motor driver controls the two drive motors.
Components

items: Arduino Uno or compatible board
HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor
L298N motor-driver module
Two geared DC motors, wheels, and a caster wheel
Robot chassis
Battery pack suitable for the motors
Jumper wires and a common ground connection

blocks.text: Circuit connections

items: HC-SR04 VCC to Arduino 5V, GND to GND, Trig to pin 9, and Echo to pin 10.
L298N IN1, IN2, IN3, and IN4 to Arduino pins 2, 3, 4, and 5.
Connect the left and right motors to the L298N output terminals.
Connect the motor battery to the L298N power input according to the module and motor ratings.
Connect Arduino GND, sensor GND, and motor-driver GND together. Never power the motors directly from an Arduino I/O pin.

blocks.text: How the robot decides

items: Send a short ultrasonic pulse.
Measure how long the echo takes to return.
Convert the travel time into distance.
Drive forward when the distance is greater than the safety threshold.
Stop, reverse briefly, and turn when an obstacle is too close.

blocks.text: Arduino code
Test safely

items: Lift the wheels off the ground for the first motor-direction test.
If one wheel spins backward, swap that motor’s two output wires.
Place the robot on a clear floor and begin with a low motor voltage.
Adjust the 20 cm threshold and turning delay for the robot’s speed and chassis.
Keep wires away from wheels and disconnect the battery before changing connections.

blocks.text: This program uses a simple fixed right turn. A later version can mount the sensor on a servo, compare open space on both sides, add speed control with PWM, or use additional sensors for smoother navigation.
